name: TPS76333DBVR
title: TPS763 150 mA, 10 V low-dropout linear regulator, fixed 1.6 V to 5.0 V or adjustable output
summary: The TPS763 is a family of CMOS low-dropout regulators in a 5-pin SOT-23 that run from 2.7 V to 10 V and deliver up to 150 mA, with fixed outputs from 1.6 V to 5.0 V or an adjustable version (TPS76301) set by two resistors. Every part number ships from either of two silicon sources, a legacy chip and a new chip, told apart by the fab source (CSO) on the packing label; the two differ in accuracy, dropout, quiescent current, ratings and capacitor needs. The new chip adds soft start, an active output pull-down and stability with small ceramic capacitors, while the legacy chip wants 4.7 µF or more with 0.3 Ω to 10 Ω ESR. Both have an active-high enable, a brick-wall current limit and thermal shutdown; TPS76333DBVR is the 3.3 V version on a 3000-piece reel.

pins.name: IN
pins.function: Supply input. Fit a capacitor of 1 µF or more from IN to ground.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable, active high: above the high threshold the regulator runs, below the low threshold it is off. On the new chip, EN is tied to VIN when it is not used.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input of the adjustable version (TPS76301): the tap of the resistor divider that sets the output voltage.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Regulated output. Fit a capacitor of 2.2 µF or more from OUT to ground; its effective value after derating must stay above 1 µF.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The regulator between a supply and its load, enabled permanently by tying EN to IN. CIN decouples the input and COUT stabilises the output. R1 and R2 form the divider into FB that sets the output on the adjustable TPS76301; the fixed versions use an internal divider and have NC on pin 4. The design example takes 5.3 V in to 3.3 V out at up to 150 mA.

parts.note: upper divider resistor, adjustable version only
lower divider resistor, adjustable version only

notes: CIN and COUT are the minimum values for IN and OUT; R2 = 169 kΩ sets a divider current near 7 µA.

circuits.title: TPS76301 adjustable regulator programming
circuits.description: The adjustable TPS76301 with its output set by R1 and R2 into FB. A logic signal on EN switches it: 0.5 V or less turns it off, 2 V or more turns it on. A 1 µF capacitor decouples the input; the output capacitor is 4.7 µF with 1 Ω of compensation series resistance (CSR).

circuits.title: Reverse current protection with a Schottky diode
circuits.description: A Schottky diode from OUT back to IN, in parallel with the pass transistor's body diode, carries any current pushed back from output toward input, so that current bypasses the regulator. CIN and COUT decouple the input and output.
notes: EN and pin 4 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Reverse current prevention with a diode before the regulator
circuits.description: A Schottky diode in series with the supply, ahead of IN, blocks current flowing back from the regulator into the source. The input capacitor sits after the diode, at IN; COUT decouples the output.
notes: EN and pin 4 are not part of this circuit.

operation.text: Each orderable number is built on one of two dies. The legacy chip comes from fab source SFB and the new chip from RFAB; the CSO field on the packing label says which. The new chip adds an internal soft start that limits inrush current and allows a smaller input capacitor, an output pull-down, and overshoot pull-down protection.

EN is active high. The output turns on above the EN high-level threshold and off below the low-level threshold. Where no separate on/off control is needed, EN is connected to IN. Pulling EN low also switches on an internal circuit that discharges the output.

Dropout voltage is VIN - VOUT at the rated 150 mA with the pass transistor fully on, working as a switch in its ohmic region. It sets the lowest input that still holds the output in regulation; below it the output follows the input down. In this CMOS part the dropout is the on-resistance of the pass device times the current, so it scales down at lighter loads.

Overload protection is a brick-wall limit: in an overload the output current is held at ICL and the output voltage is no longer regulated. The pass device then dissipates (VIN - VOUT) × ICL. If that heats the die to thermal shutdown, the part turns off and restarts once cool, cycling between limit and shutdown for as long as the fault stays.

The output turns off when the junction reaches TSD(shutdown) and back on when it cools to TSD(reset). The die cools quickly, so the part may cycle on and off until dissipation drops. A large VIN - VOUT or a large output capacitor charging at start-up can trip it before start-up finishes, and with the load near ICL the output may oscillate before turning off. Junction temperature is to stay within the recommended maximum; running into shutdown repeatedly shortens life, and the protection does not replace heat sinking.

The new chip pulls its output down when it is disabled (VEN < VEN(LOW)) and when VIN is between 1.0 V and 2.7 V. The pull-down is not meant to discharge a large output capacitance after the input has collapsed: current then flows from output to input and can damage the part.

Normal: VIN above VOUT(nom) + VDO, load below the current limit, junction below shutdown, and EN having risen past its rising threshold without since falling below the falling one. Dropout: VIN below VOUT(nom) + VDO with the rest normal; the output tracks the input and line and load transients give large deviations. When the input rises out of steady dropout, the output can overshoot briefly while the pass device returns to its linear region. Disabled: EN below the low threshold, VIN below 2.7 V or junction above shutdown; the pass device is off and the output is discharged.

The output needs at least 4.7 µF between OUT and GND with an ESR from 0.3 Ω to 10 Ω; larger values are fine while the ESR stays under 10 Ω. Solid tantalum, aluminium electrolytic and multilayer ceramic types all qualify if they meet this, and most 4.7 µF surface-mount tantalum capacitors do. The stable CSR range depends on load current and on any added ceramic capacitance. An input capacitor is optional; 0.047 µF or more of ceramic close to the part improves transient response and noise rejection, and a larger electrolytic may be needed for fast, large load steps with the source several inches away.

The new chip is stable with low-ESR ceramic capacitors on input and output; X7R, X5R and C0G dielectrics hold their value over temperature, Y5V is advised against. Output ESR must stay under 1 Ω over -40 °C to 150 °C and 0 mA to 150 mA; where a higher-ESR capacitor is already used, a low-ESR 100 nF ceramic is added right at OUT. Ceramic capacitance can drop by up to 50 % with voltage and temperature, and the recommended values allow for that; the effective output capacitance must stay above 1 µF. An input capacitor is not needed for stability but helps with reactive sources, transients, ripple and PSRR, and is used when the source impedance exceeds 0.5 Ω. The output capacitor improves dynamic response and must lie within the recommended range.

Current forced from OUT to IN flows through the body diode of the pass transistor, is not limited inside the part, and can damage it or reduce its life. It arises when a large COUT holds the output up as the input collapses at light load, when the output is driven before the input is up, or when the output is held above the input; each can break the VOUT ≤ VIN + 0.3 V limit. Where it can happen, external protection is used: a Schottky diode from OUT to IN, or, more commonly at high input voltage, a diode in series ahead of IN.
On the adjustable version a capacitor CFF from OUT to FB improves transient response, noise and PSRR. It is not needed for stability; a larger CFF lengthens start-up.

Dissipation is roughly (VIN - VOUT) × IOUT, so the lowest input that keeps regulation gives the least heat. Other heat sources are kept away from the regulator. RθJA depends strongly on the board: copper area, weight and plane placement. The table figure comes from the JEDEC standard board and is a relative measure; ψJT and ψJB estimate junction temperature from a measured package-top or board temperature and depend little on copper area.

A very large or very fast input step can shut the new chip down briefly, for up to a few hundred microseconds after the edge. A smaller step, a slower edge, or both avoid it; the step size against slew rate limit is given as a curve.

R1 and R2 are chosen for about 7 µA through the divider: R2 = 169 kΩ, then R1 from the equation. Smaller resistors work but only waste power; larger ones let leakage at FB add output error. A fixed version has the divider inside and draws less quiescent current.
A larger output capacitor reduces overshoot and undershoot but makes the recovery last longer.
The new chip is designed to run from an input supply of 2.4 V to 18 V. The input is fed from a low-impedance source; with a noisy supply, more low-ESR input capacitance improves output noise.

Input and output capacitors go as close to the part as possible, connections use copper planes for heat, and thermal vias round the part spread the heat. For the DBV package, CIN goes beside pins 1 and 2 and COUT beside pin 5, both returning to a ground plane.
